supplant

suh-PLANT -- from Latin supplantare ('to trip up'), from sub- ('under') + planta ('sole of the foot'). · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To supplant is to take the place of something or someone, especially by force, scheming, or gradual displacement.

Within a single decade, streaming services had almost entirely supplanted the neighborhood video rental store.

Example

The ambitious deputy spent years quietly building alliances until he finally supplanted his own mentor as head of the department.

That deliberate, often gradual takeover of someone else's place -- not a simple, friendly handoff -- is exactly what it means to supplant someone.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

replace: Replace is the neutral, everyday word for putting one thing where another was, with no hint of pushing anything out. To supplant is to replace by force or slow scheming: whatever held the place before is shoved aside or gradually crowded out.

oust: To oust is to throw someone out of a position -- the story ends with the removal itself. To supplant goes a step further: the one who supplants not only pushes a rival out but steps into the emptied place.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

preserve: to keep something safe and unchanged

reinstate: to bring something or someone back to a former position

Where it sits · how deliberate the takeover is — displace → supplant → usurp

displace vs. supplant: Displace is milder than supplant: things get displaced by impersonal forces -- a flood, a new highway, rising rents -- and simply end up out of place, while to supplant is to push something aside on purpose and claim its position.

usurp vs. supplant: Usurp is more extreme than supplant: one who supplants may rise by slow, quiet scheming, but a usurper wrongfully seizes a throne or an office outright, grabbing power that was never rightfully theirs.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — sup-

prefix — sup-: under (the form Latin sub- takes before a p)

root — plant

root — plant: sole of the foot (from Latin planta)

Put it together

Put it together: Supplant is built from sup- ('under' -- the form Latin sub- takes before a p) + plant ('sole of the foot,' from Latin planta) -- it originally meant to trip someone by the sole of the foot, and the word kept that sense of knocking someone out of their place.

Use the root in a new word: plantar

Use the root in a new word: plantar: The runner was sidelined for weeks by a painful case of plantar fasciitis in her heel.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Supplant almost always implies that the newcomer forced out or gradually replaced whatever came before it -- it's a stronger, more pointed word than simply 'replace.'
